newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO secret summit comes up short of deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO secret summit comes up short of deal.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat met secretly under the cover of darkness early on Sunday but failed to break the deadlock on a self-rule deal for Hebron.

News of the four-hour meeting at the Israeli-Gaza Strip border leaked out hours after it ended at 6 a.m. Netanyahu said he thought it would help build confidence if he and Arafat shunned the media spotlight.

Despite the failure to clinch a deal, both sides reported progress. U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross, who took part in the secret meeting, had been scrambling to arrange a summit in hopes of ironing out a deal on the West Bank town.
"I met with Yasser Arafat at the Erez junction," Netanyahu told businessmen in Tel Aviv in the afternoon. "We are making progress but we still haven't reached full agreement on all the issues."

An agreement would give Palestinians self-rule in most of Hebron, a volatile town of 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jews. Security issues and other concerns over the last 10 months have delayed the Israeli handover to Arafat's PLO.

"An Arafat-Netanyahu summit took place at Erez from 2 a.m. to 6 a.m. Both leaders discussed all disputed issues but the leaders were unable to bridge all gaps," Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
"Contacts and efforts will continue until we close a deal," he said. Palestinians said another summit could take place later on Sunday.

Chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said that despite the snags, a deal would be signed on Monday in the West Bank town of Jericho to station 210 international observers in Hebron once Israeli troops redeploy.
He said the observers would come from Denmark, Italy, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
Under a 1995 interim agreement, international observers are to be deployed in the town to maintain order, protect residents and monitor violations of the agreement.
Some 400 Palestinian policemen are due to deploy in the Palestinian-ruled part of Hebron.
Officials for the two sides, who last week predicted an imminent deal, accused each other of causing a delay.
"Mr Arafat isn't ready to close the deal on the basis of the agreements that have already been made," Netanyahu's adviser Dore Gold told Reuters.

Palestinians say the central issue blocking an accord is Israel's refusal to commit to a timetable for three further West Bank pullbacks in mostly rural areas after Hebron, as stipulated in previous peace deals.
"There won't be an agreement unless there will be a commitment on the three phases," Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi told Israeli army radio on Sunday. Erekat said other issues also had to be resolved.

Underscoring tensions, witnesses said that as news of the meeting leaked out, unidentified assailants hurled a petrol bomb in front of a building inhabited by Jews in the town. No one was hurt and no damage was caused.
Elsewhere in the West Bank, Jewish settlers began removing seven mobile homes from a hilltop on Sunday under a deal reached with government officials.
Their bid on Friday to set up a new outpost without government approval near the settlement of Beit El, north of the Palestinian town of Ramallah, drew sharp PLO condemnation.
The settlers said they had struck a deal with the government under which they would remove the caravans in exchange for a meeting with Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai to discuss expanding Beit El.
